newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US on Buba comments, Japan trade.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US on Buba comments, Japan trade.

text.p: Dollar/mark closed lower after a barrage of comments by German central bankers, but dollar/yen firmed slightly despite signs the dollar's recent strength is helping Japanese exporters.

Japan's Finance Ministry on Monday reported its merchandise trade surplus with the US expanded in October for the first time since February 1995, with a weak yen cited for helping Japanese automobile manufacturers boost exports.
A rising Japanese trade surplus risks increased friction with the US and would usually weigh on dollar/yen as Japan accumulates surplus dollars from the sale of exports.

Meanwhile, the dollar fell to 1.5007/17 marks, after starting at 1.5055/65, hurt principally by U.S. wire service reports that Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke told reporters he saw no reason for the dollar to appreciate.
The dollar briefly dipped to 1.4985 marks but stop-loss sell orders reported below 1.4980 remained out of reach.

The greenback later reclaimed some of the lost ground when Welteke subsequently said the reports got his comments wrong, telling journalists the Bundesbank wanted to see a "more stable" and "stronger" dollar.

"It's just contrary statements pushing the dollar back and forth," said John Nelson, a senior vice president at ABN-Amro Bank in Chicago. He noted that the dollar traded relatively uneventfully against the mark, despite a sharp rally by the mark against the yen.

Traders said the dollar started weakening in European trade, when the mark firmed after Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler warned Eurpean countries not to use creative accounting to meet tough fiscal conditions for joining Europe's proposed single currency in 1999.

The mark, currently Europe's anchor currency, is scheduled to be replaced by a weaker single currency, called the euro, in 1999. The German unit often strengthens when tensions threaten to delay progress towards currency union.

The mark gave little back against the dollar after a third Bundesbank member, Hans-Juergen Krupp, said the guidelines for participation in European Monetary Union do not require budget deficit and public debt targets to be hit exactly.
"There are obviously two different sides of the story, even out of the Bundesbank," said David Solin, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"The question is how much input does the Bundesbank really have into this process? I think when push comes to shove it's a political issue, not a monetary issue," Solin added.
In other trade, the pound rose to a fresh four-year high at $1.6725, and closed at $1.6703/13, up from $1.6665/75 at the open.
The dollar fell to 1.2660/70 Swiss francs, from 1.2717/27 Swiss and it rose to Canadian $1.3430/35 from C$1.3402/07 late Friday.
